items.value: Maximum marks = 150
items.reasoning: He scores 30 and falls short by 30, so the pass mark is 30 + 30 = 60. The pass mark is 40% of the maximum, so 0.40 x M = 60, giving M = 150. Checking: 40% of 150 is 60, and 60 - 30 = 30, exactly the stated shortfall. The other options fail this check: 40% of 100 is 40, of 120 is 48 and of 300 is 120, none of which is 60.

items.value: 6 boys are wearing both shirt and pants (full uniform)
items.reasoning: Since no boy is without a shirt and/or pants, every one of the 19 boys wears at least one of the two items, so the union of the two sets is 19. By the inclusion-exclusion principle, |shirts| + |pants| - |both| = |union|, i.e. 11 + 14 - x = 19, so x = 6. Six boys therefore wear both, which is the full uniform.

items.value: Assumptions 2 and 3 are valid; assumption 1 is not
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 is invalid: the passage says the problem is 'more severe' for developing countries, a comparison that presupposes climate change is a challenge for developed countries too, and it adds that 'most countries' are striving to address it. Assumption 3 is plainly valid: the passage opens by saying all actions involve costs and that funding is vital for adaptation and mitigation plans, which is exactly the claim that ways and means of finance must be found. Assumption 2 is the item's pivot and is taken as valid: the passage ties climate change directly to India's 'need to finance development' and to addressing the issue in a 'comprehensive and integrated manner' with limited resources, which presupposes it is both a development issue and a complex policy issue. Runner-up: B (3 only), which wins if one applies a strict assumption test and holds that 'complex policy issue' is a conclusion drawn from the passage rather than something the passage takes for granted. (The passage as printed reads 'as real threat', missing an article; this is preserved as printed and does not affect the answer.)

items.value: Access to clean cooking gas can reduce premature deaths in poor households
items.reasoning: The passage attributes more than 10 lakh premature deaths a year to household air pollution from polluting cooking fuels, with the poor at greatest risk, and names LPG, natural gas and electricity as the clean alternatives. The direct inference is that giving poor households access to clean cooking gas would cut those deaths. Option A is contradicted, since the number using solid fuels has been static for nearly 30 years and awareness is never mentioned; option B overstates with 'will solve' and introduces subsidies, which the passage does not discuss; option C is a policy prescription about imports and electricity generation that the passage nowhere supports.

items.value: A happy world is not possible without science
items.reasoning: The load-bearing phrase is that science 'opens up as nothing else can, the vision of a possible happy world' — that is, no other agency can do it, which is precisely the claim that a happy world is not possible without science. Option B is contradicted by the passage's own qualification that science 'has its dangers, but so has every great thing', so science is not the only major threat. Option A reduces the claim to a mere 'dream' and drops the exclusivity that the passage insists on, and option D flatly contradicts a passage that calls science 'in its very nature a liberator'.

items.value: Melting of Arctic summer ice is changing geopolitics
items.reasoning: The passage says the prospect of an ice-free summer has prompted the countries with an Arctic coastline to 'scramble for great chunks of the melting ocean', with no legal regime of the Antarctic Treaty kind to restrain them — a geopolitical consequence of the melting ice, which is exactly option B. Option A fails because the scramble is confined to countries with an Arctic coastline, which India does not have. Option C ('will solve the world's future problem of resource crunch') is far stronger than anything the passage claims, and option D compares Arctic and Antarctic resource endowments, a comparison the passage never makes — it contrasts their legal regimes, not their reserves.

items.value: India's food security obligations collide with its trade commitments
items.reasoning: The passage sets India's PDS, which rests on minimum support prices and public stockholding, against Article 6 of the WTO Agriculture Agreement, which caps such support at 10 per cent of the value of agricultural production, and notes the subsidy may exceed that cap in some years. That is a direct clash between a food-security instrument and a trade obligation. Options A and B are prescriptions the passage never makes — it describes a conflict without recommending that the PDS be revised or that India leave the WTO — and option D restates a background fact rather than the message the passage is built to convey.

items.value: Only assumption 2 is valid
items.reasoning: Assumption 2 is valid: the passage contrasts a system built to supply a compliant workforce with 'a narrow set of capabilities' against an economic environment that is now 'complex, volatile and globally interconnected', which presupposes that today's learners need new-age skill-sets. Assumption 1 is invalid — the passage never claims the education system is why India remains a developing country, and it points out that the same model spread from 19th-century Europe around the world. Assumption 3 is invalid and unrelated: the passage says nothing about Indians studying abroad, and its criticism of factory-like schooling would not support calling foreign systems a 'perfect reflection' of their societies.

items.value: There is no single perfect diet or one-size solution for obesity
items.reasoning: The passage lists the many ways in which people differ — ethnicity, genetics, family history, gender, age, health, lifestyle, food tolerances — and concludes that 'we really cannot reduce so many complexities into one diet or diet book', which it says explains why diets fail to curb obesity. That is option D. Option A misreads the first line, which calls the practice of dieting, not obesity, an epidemic. Option B merely restates a phrase from the opening sentence rather than drawing the inference the passage builds towards, and option C is contradicted by the closing sentence, which says weight can be controlled once reasons are addressed and habits permanently changed.

items.value: Preserving crop genetic diversity is an insurance against the effects of climate change
items.reasoning: The passage's argument is that monoculture — reliance on genetic sameness — lets a single disease or pest wipe out large parts of world food production, and that this risk is magnified by a warming climate bringing floods, droughts and crop diseases to new latitudes. The message that follows is that genetic diversity is the hedge against exactly those effects. Option B inverts the passage, which warns against monoculture rather than endorsing it; option C introduces genetically modified crops, which the passage never mentions; option D picks up incidental detail about Asia and North America and inflates it into a claim about the 'worst sufferers' that the passage does not make.

items.value: Original cost price = ₹ 30
items.reasoning: If the cost price is C, the profit at ₹ 40 is 40 - C and the loss at ₹ 20 is C - 20; equal percentages on the same cost mean equal amounts, so 40 - C = C - 20, giving 2C = 60 and C = ₹ 30. Checking: profit and loss are both ₹ 10 on a cost of ₹ 30, that is one-third or about 33.3 per cent each way, so the percentages do match. In general the cost is the mean of the two selling prices, (40 + 20)/2 = 30.

items.value: 8 equilateral triangles
items.reasoning: Equally spaced points on a circle form an equilateral triangle only when the three vertices divide the circumference into three equal arcs, i.e. when consecutive vertices are 24/3 = 8 steps apart. Numbering the points 0 to 23, the triangles are {0,8,16}, {1,9,17}, ... , {7,15,23} — the starting index can be any of 0 to 7, after which the sets repeat. That gives exactly 8 distinct equilateral triangles.

items.value: 25/3/96 — the series advances by 28 days each time
items.reasoning: The gaps are constant: 4 Dec 1995 to 1 Jan 1996 is 27 + 1 = 28 days, 1 Jan to 29 Jan is 28 days, and 29 Jan to 26 Feb is 2 + 26 = 28 days. Adding 28 days to 26 Feb 1996 requires care because 1996 is a leap year, so February has 29 days: three days take us to 29 February, and the remaining 25 days give 25 March 1996. Answering 24/3/96 would be the error of treating February as having 28 days.

items.value: Each square has area 1 sq cm (side 1 cm)
items.reasoning: With three rows of four squares of side s and no gaps, the rectangle measures 4s by 3s. Its diagonal is \(\sqrt{(4s)^2 + (3s)^2} = \sqrt{25s^2} = 5s\), and this is given as 5 cm, so s = 1 cm and each square has area 1 sq cm. As a check, the rectangle is 4 cm by 3 cm, a 3-4-5 right triangle on each half, and the twelve unit squares fill its area of 12 sq cm exactly.
